data.claim: Python re backtracks exponentially on nested repeats and cannot be interrupted, so a pre-check must refuse them
data.probe_output: 7.3s for 27 chars (doubles per char); guard refuses it
data.question: Can a user regex hang ddflow search?

evidence.note: R-search-redos CONFIRMED: unguarded (a+)+$ takes 7.3s on 27 chars; check_regex refuses it
D-readme-current: README section Searching everything + command table; D-no-duplicates n/a
full suite pytest -n 48: 4685 passed, 1 skipped (incl. tests/test_view_search.py 10, test_mcp_parity)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_walk` only refuses a repeat nested inside another when the inner repeat is unbounded OR its upper bound exceeds `MAX_NESTED` (100):

```python
if in_repeat and hi > 1 and (unbounded or hi > MAX_NESTED):
    raise SearchError(...)
```

That leaves every inner bounded repeat with `2 <= hi <= 100` allowed, e.g. `(a{1,2})+`. This is the textbook exponential-backtracking case (equivalent to `(a|aa)+`) — the check catches the `BRANCH`-spelled form but not the bounded-repeat spelling, even though the module docstring claims "no catastrophic backtracking". Concretely: `check_regex("(a{1,2})+b")` walks to the inner `MAX_REPEAT` with `hi=2`, `hi > 1` is true but `unbounded` is false and `2 > 100` is false, so it compiles and runs. `_scan` then executes `rx.search(d.text[:MAX_SCAN])` on the raw record text, but its `deadline`/`BUDGET_S` guard only runs *between* records (`if time.monotonic() > deadline` in the loop), so a single `search()` call cannot be interrupted. A session summary, bug evidence, or log payload containing ~60 consecutive `a` characters makes that one call perform roughly Fib(60) ≈ 2.5e12 backtracking steps (hours), hanging the request; `MAX_SCAN=2000` permits up to 2000 such characters. The stated acceptance ("a pathological regex is refused or bounded") is not met for this pattern.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:check_regex / _walk (the nested-repeat rule)

chunk_findings.detail: In `_walk`, `ASSERT`, `ASSERT_NOT`, and `ATOMIC_GROUP` are handled together via `_walk(c, av[1], ...)`. That is correct only for the assertions, whose `av` is `(direction, subpattern)`. For an atomic group `(?>...)` the parser node is `(ATOMIC_GROUP, subpattern)` — `av` *is* the sub-pattern list (this is why the compiler does `self._compile(code, av)` for `ATOMIC_GROUP` but `self._compile(code, av[1])` for `ASSERT`). So `av[1]` indexes into the sub-pattern's element list instead of using it. With `check_regex("(?>a)")`: `av == SubPattern([(LITERAL, 97)])`, `av[1]` raises `IndexError` (for `(?>ab)`, `av[1]` is `(LITERAL, 98)` and the subsequent `for op, av in nodes` raises `TypeError`). This exception is raised outside the `try` in `check_regex`, so a valid regex containing an atomic group crashes the search instead of compiling (or being refused) — the refusal contract is violated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:_walk (ATOMIC_GROUP branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes the parity suite green by exempting `search` instead of exposing it, which is the opposite of the stated acceptance ("MCP parity and budget tests green", "MCP: add a search mode to the consolidated read tool (or one short ddflow_search) within the tools/list byte budget"). Concretely: with `ddflow search` registered (viewers_search.py) and `"search"`/`("search",)` added to the exemption maps, the test that asserts "every CLI command is either MCP-reachable or listed as exempt" passes while `tools/list` still contains no search capability, so an MCP client doing a read cannot search sessions, session notes/summaries, prompts, or the event log at all. The stated workaround in the exemption is also factually wrong: the intent text explicitly says `ddflow_recall` sources decisions/lessons/memories/research/bugs/items/prompts and that "nothing searches session notes/summaries or the event log", so the "(agents use ddflow_recall)" justification does not cover exactly the sources this command was added for. This is a real behavioural gap masked by a test exemption, not merely a deferred nicety: run the parity suite and it reports green although the MCP surface the acceptance criterion requires is absent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_parity.py:38 (and :168, `("search",)` entry)

chunk_findings.detail: The intent enumerates the public filter surface as `--kind, --state, --phase, --agent, --since, --limit, --json`, but this test (and only this test) exercises an `--owner` flag and no test anywhere exercises `--agent`. `test_owner_filter_is_the_session_agent` calls `_search(repo, "fennel", "--owner", "alice")`; if the CLI is built to the documented contract with `--agent` and no `--owner`, `run_cli(... "--owner", "alice")` exits 3 (unknown option) and `_search` yields `body = {}` (helpers only `json.loads` when output starts with `{`), so `body["rows"]` raises `KeyError` — the test errors rather than passing. Conversely, if `--owner` is the real flag, then the documented `--agent` filter does not exist and the "filters narrow" acceptance criterion for agent filtering is not covered by any test. Either the test contradicts the specified interface or the specified interface is absent; the two cannot both be right.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_view_search.py:test_owner_filter_is_the_session_agent

chunk_findings.detail: The `_walk` guard only refuses an alternation when `in_open` is set, and `in_open` is set only by an *unbounded* repeat (`in_open or unbounded`). An alternation inside a **bounded** repeat therefore passes. Because the pattern is bounded, the `if in_repeat and hi > 1 and (unbounded or hi > MAX_NESTED)` check also does not fire at top level (`in_repeat` is False). So `(a|aa){1,1000}` (and even `(a|aa){1,100}`) is accepted by `check_regex` — yet bounded repetition over an alternation of unequal-length branches is exactly the classic exponential-backtracking family. Worse, `BUDGET_S` is only tested in `_scan` *between* documents (`if time.monotonic() > deadline` before each `d`), so a single `rx.search(d.text[:MAX_SCAN])` can run arbitrarily long; the 5 s budget cannot interrupt one call. Concrete repro: `ddflow search '(a|aa){1,1000}b' --regex` against a record whose text contains a run of ~2000 `a`s (within `MAX_SCAN`) with no `b`. The match fails, the engine backtracks over every 1/2 partition of the run (Fibonacci-like count, astronomically large), and the process hangs (or blows the Python recursion limit uncaught) instead of being refused or bounded. The acceptance requirement "a pathological regex is refused or bounded" is not met.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_walk` (BRANCH handling) and `_scan` (BUDGET_S deadline)

chunk_findings.detail: `_walk` treats `ATOMIC_GROUP` like `ASSERT`/`ASSERT_NOT` and recurses into `av[1]`. In `re._parser`, `ASSERT` is stored as `(ASSERT, (dir, subpattern))`, but an atomic group is stored as `(ATOMIC_GROUP, subpattern)` — the argument is the subpattern list itself, not a wrapper tuple. So for a valid, harmless atomic-group pattern the walker indexes into the wrong thing: `(?>)`-style input `(?>a)` gives `av = [(LITERAL, 97)]` and `av[1]` raises `IndexError: list index out of range`; with two-or-more items, `av[1]` is a `(op, arg)` tuple and `for op, av in nodes` raises `TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable _NamedIntConstant`. Only `re.error`/`RecursionError`/`OverflowError` are caught in `check_regex`, so the exception escapes as a traceback rather than either searching or a clean `SearchError`. Concrete repro: `ddflow search '(?>a)' --regex` crashes instead of returning results or a refusal message.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_walk` (ATOMIC_GROUP handling)

chunk_findings.detail: The change records the same exemption twice, in two registries with mutually exclusive meanings. `NOT_EXPOSED: dict[str, str]` is documented as the set of "CLI commands deliberately NOT exposed" — the other entries there (`mcp`, `approve`) are withheld permanently for correctness/safety reasons. The entry added here for `"search"` is not that: its own reason says the command *will* be exposed by the later task `B-view-mcp-list`. At the same time `("search",)` is added to the tuple-keyed coverage registry (the one holding `("list",)`, `("adopt",)`, `("init",)`), which is the registry that already means "deferred, will be covered by another MCP tool". So a brand-new, user-facing command is now exempted in both places, which means the "MCP parity tests green" acceptance is satisfied by disabling the parity check rather than by delivering the MCP search mode the intent requires: an MCP client still cannot search sessions/logs. Concretely, whichever assertion iterates `NOT_EXPOSED` (by plain command name) and whichever iterates the tuple registry (by command path) will both skip `search`, so when `B-view-mcp-list` lands, nothing will fail if the MCP search mode is missing or broken. If the parity test treats the two registries as disjoint categories (permanent non-exposure vs. coverage-by-another-tool) — the only reading consistent with their docstrings and existing contents — the overlap makes the classification ambiguous and the assertion unsatisfiable. The deferred-search exemption belongs only in the coverage registry; the `NOT_EXPOSED` insertion is semantically wrong and should be removed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_parity.py:39,168 (`NOT_EXPOSED["search"]` and `("search",)` exemption)

chunk_findings.detail: The test narrows by agent with `--owner alice` / `--owner bob`, but the intent for this change enumerates the search filters as `--kind, --state, --phase, --agent, --since, --limit, --json` — there is no `--owner` flag, and the test is itself named "owner filter is the session agent." Two outcomes are both defects: (a) if the CLI implements the documented `--agent` flag, `run_cli(repo, "search", "fennel", "--owner", "alice")` hits an unknown option, exits 3, and both `assert body["rows"]` and the Bob assertion fail; (b) if the CLI really implements `--owner` instead, then the spec-mandated `--agent` filter does not exist and the "filters narrow by agent" acceptance criterion is never exercised. In either case the agent-filter behavior is asserted against a flag that the change never documents.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_view_search.py:test_owner_filter_is_the_session_agent

chunk_findings.detail: The BRANCH guard now fires whenever an alternation sits *anywhere* inside a repeat whose max is greater than 1, without inspecting the bound. That makes the refusal unconditional on how small the repeat is, so trivially bounded patterns that cannot exhibit exponential backtracking are rejected. Concretely: `ddflow search "(ab|cd){2}" --regex` (equally `(TODO|FIXME){2}`, `(a|b){2,3}`) now exits 3 with "regex refused: an alternation inside a repeat can take exponential time", yet `{2}` admits at most 4 expansion paths and a following literal cannot force more work. Before this change the same pattern was accepted, because the guard only looked at `in_open` (unbounded repeats) and `{2}` is not unbounded (the walk sets `in_repeat` via `in_repeat or hi > 1`, and `hi == 2` here). Since the condition never looks at the magnitude of `hi` or whether the bound is finite, it also rejects patterns like `(ab|cd){2,4}`, which conflicts with the stated purpose of refusing patterns "that can take exponential time" — this is collateral over-refusal of safe, previously working regexes, not a tightening limited to pathological ones.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:172 (`if in_open or in_repeat:`)

chunk_findings.detail:
Changing the guard from `(unbounded or hi > MAX_NESTED)` to `(unbounded or lo != hi)` silently drops the `MAX_NESTED = 100` cap, so fixed-count repeats with `lo == hi` are now accepted no matter how large the count is, including when nested under a repeat. The `in_repeat` flag is propagated through `?`/`{0,1}` nodes (`in_repeat or hi > 1` is true), but those nodes' own check is skipped because of the `hi > 1` guard, so the count bound was the only thing that caught this shape.

Demonstration: `check_regex(r"((a{101})?){100}")` (equivalently `((a{101}){0,1}){100}`) walks as `MAX_REPEAT(100,100) → SUBPATTERN → MAX_REPEAT(0,1) → SUBPATTERN → MAX_REPEAT(101,101)`. At the innermost node `in_repeat` is `True`, `hi = 101 > 1`, `unbounded` is `False`, and `lo != hi` is `False` (`101 != 101` is false), so no error is raised and a compiled pattern is returned. With the old condition, `hi > MAX_NESTED` (`101 > 100`) was true and the pattern was refused.

That pattern is catastrophic: against a record containing ~2000 `a`s, each of the 100 outer iterations may consume 0 or 101 characters, so the engine explores every choice of up to 19 non-empty blocks, i.e. `sum_{k=0..19} C(100,k)` ≈ 1.3e19 backtracking paths before failing (e.g. append a trailing `b` that is absent). Because Python's `re` engine "cannot be interrupted" (per the module docstring), the `BUDGET_S = 5.0` budget is never enforced for that single match, so `ddflow search --regex '((a{101})?){100}'` over such a payload hangs instead of refusing the request with exit code 3. The deleted `MAX_NESTED` bound was the mechanism that rejected exactly these high-count nested fixed repeats, and removing it re-opens that class.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:162 (`_walk`, nested-repeat guard in `check_regex`)

chunk_findings.detail: The expanded denylist requires the CLI to reject, with exit code 3, two patterns that are not catastrophic, so `--regex` now refuses legitimate searches. `.*a.*b.*c` is polynomial (worst case on "aaaa…a" with no `b` is O(n²)/O(n³) scanning, not exponential), and `(?>a+)+b` uses an atomic group, which suppresses the very backtracking that makes `(a+)+b` explosive — it fails fast on any input. Concretely: a user searching for `.*error.*timeout.*` (same shape as `.*a.*b.*c`) gets exit code 3 "pathological regex" instead of results, contradicting the stated acceptance that "exact/regex work". The test hard-codes this over-blocking, so any implementation that actually validates patterns (or bounds them by timeout instead of statically refusing) will fail this test. (Secondary to the same edit: `(?>a+)+b` is only valid syntax on Python ≥ 3.11; requiring exactly code 3 rather than accepting the code-2 "invalid pattern" outcome conflates unsupported syntax with catastrophic backtracking, unlike the sibling test which tolerates `(0, 2, 3)` for the same construct.)
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_view_search.py::test_pathological_regex_is_refused (new entries `".*a.*b.*c"`, `"(?>a+)+b"`)
